data.title: Local people who like showing their city.
data.intro: Local City Tours is a small company of guides who grew up in or near the old city. This page says who we are and how we work.

children.text: We started with one guide and a handful of friends who asked for a walk. Now there are six of us. We lead around forty tours a week in high season, in four languages.
How we work
Groups stay small, between eight and fourteen. Every guide lives in the city and writes their own route within the same set of stops.
We do not sell on commission, we do not take you to a shop and we do not tell you where to buy a souvenir. If you ask for a restaurant, we give you two.
What we ask of you
Be at the meeting point ten minutes early. Tell us about allergies and mobility when you book. Say so if the pace is wrong, because we can change it.
Booking
Send a booking request from the Book page. We confirm by email, usually within one working day. You pay your guide on the day.

data.title: Ivy Alley Walk
data.summary: A slow loop through the narrow streets of the Old Gate quarter, with the stories behind the doors.
data.meeting_point: Lantern Square, steps of the dry fountain
data.meeting_note: Look for a green flag and a guide wearing a lanyard. We wait ten minutes after the start time.
data.accessibility: Mostly flat, but the street is cobbled and there are two short flights of steps near the end. A step-free route is possible on a private tour.
data.included:
A local guide for the whole walk
A paper map of the old city with our favorite stops marked
A water refill stop halfway
A short list of places to eat nearby
data.route:
Lantern Square|We meet, check the group and agree a pace.
Cooper's Row|The old workshops, and why the doors are so low.
Ivy Passage|The narrowest street in the quarter. We stop for photos.
Bakers' Steps|A rest, a story about the lantern lighters and a look over the roofs.
Gate Square|We finish at the old gate. The guide suggests where to go next.
data.intro: Most visitors walk past Ivy Passage without seeing it. We go in, slowly, and talk about who lived and worked on this street.

data.title: River Steps and Bridges
data.summary: Down to the water by the old mill steps, then across three bridges that each tell a different part of the story.
data.meeting_note: We stand at the bottom of the steps, next to the iron mooring posts.
data.accessibility: There are 60 steps down to the river and a gentle slope back up. We take it slowly and stop often. Not suitable for wheelchairs.
data.included:
A local guide
A printed map of the river walk
A coffee stop at a family-run kiosk (one drink each)
data.route:
Mill Steps|The mills that once powered the quarter.
Lower Bridge|Where the market boats used to unload.
Stone Bridge|The oldest crossing. We talk about the floods.
River Wall|A flat stretch with views of the dome.
Kiosk stop|Coffee or tea, and a seat.
data.intro: The river is easy to miss from the main streets. This walk puts it at the center and keeps the pace gentle.

data.title: Lantern Evening Walk
data.summary: The old streets as the lamps come on, with fewer people and a lot more shadow.
data.meeting_point: Lantern Square, steps of the dry fountain
data.meeting_note: Look for the guide holding a small brass lantern.
data.accessibility: Streets are cobbled and some are poorly lit. Bring a small flashlight if you prefer. Mostly flat.
data.included:
A local guide
A lantern for the group to follow
A hot drink or a cold one at the end (one each)
data.route:
Lantern Square|We meet as the first lamps are lit.
Cooper's Row|Quiet at this hour. We talk about the night watch.
Ivy Passage|Best seen with the lamps on.
Gate Square|We finish with a drink at a corner bar the guide trusts.
data.intro: A shorter walk for the end of the day. We keep to the quiet streets and finish with a drink.

data.title: Market and Plates
data.summary: A morning in the covered market and five small plates at the stalls and counters locals actually use.
data.meeting_note: We meet under the south arch of the bell tower. Please arrive hungry.
data.accessibility: Flat, with a lot of standing at counters. Seats are available at two of the five stops. Tell us about allergies and diets when you book.
data.included:
Five tastings at five different stalls and counters
Water and one glass of local wine or juice
A local guide who knows the stallholders
A printed list of what we ate and where to buy it
data.route:
Bell Tower Square|We meet and talk through the morning.
Covered market|Cheese, olives and bread from the same family for three generations.
Fish counter|A small plate cooked in front of us.
Cooper's Row|A bakery with a queue before eight.
Corner counter|A last plate and a sit down.
data.intro: You eat at counters, standing up, the way people here do. The guide knows who to ask for what.

data.title: Cellar and Cheese Evening
data.summary: Two cellars, one cheese counter and a long table at the end. A calm evening with local wine and plain food.
data.meeting_note: Our office has a blue door. The guide waits on the step.
data.accessibility: One cellar has 14 narrow steps down. The second is at street level. Ask us if the steps are a problem and we will swap it.
data.included:
Four wines or juices, poured by the people who made them
Cheese, bread and cured meats (a vegetarian board on request)
A local guide
A card with the names of what you tasted
data.route:
Cooper's Row|We meet and walk to the first cellar.
Lower cellar|Two wines and a talk about how the quarter stored them.
Cheese counter|Three cheeses and the story of the dairy.
Long table|Bread, a last glass and time to ask questions.
data.intro: An evening for adults. We go slowly, we sit down and nobody is hurried.

data.title: Dome and Rooftops
data.summary: The main sights, in a sensible order, with a climb to the dome terrace for the best view of the old city.
data.meeting_note: Look for a green flag by the old gate. The guide has a lanyard and a folded map.
data.accessibility: The terrace is up 220 steps and is optional. The rest of the tour is flat, with some cobbles. Entry to the terrace is paid at the door, about $8.
data.included:
A local guide
A route that avoids the longest lines
A short break at a courtyard café (drinks not included)
A paper map with the day's route
data.route:
Gate Square|Introductions and how the old city grew.
Cathedral steps|The facade and what the carvings show.
Dome terrace|The climb is optional. The view is the reason we came.
Old Exchange|A quiet courtyard and a coffee break.
Bell Tower Square|We finish at the market edge.
data.intro: If you have one morning, this is the one. We cover the big sights in a sensible order and avoid the worst crowds.

data.title: Terrace at Sunset
data.summary: Three viewpoints over the old city, timed for the last hour of light, with a sit-down at the final one.
data.meeting_note: We meet under the south arch. Look for the green flag.
data.accessibility: One steep ramp and about 80 steps in total. There is a bench at every viewpoint. Not suitable for wheelchairs.
data.included:
A local guide
A soft drink or glass of wine at the last viewpoint
A photo spot at each stop (the guide will take your picture)
data.route:
Bell Tower Square|We set out as the light turns yellow.
Stone terrace|The first view of the dome and the river.
Garden wall|A quiet spot most visitors never find.
Roof terrace|A seat, a drink and the last of the light.
data.intro: The best light in the old city is in the last hour of the day. We plan the route around it.

data.title: Why we cap groups at twelve
data.excerpt: Our biggest tour has fourteen places. Most have eight to twelve. Here is why we do not go higher.

children.text: In a narrow street, a group of twelve fits on one side and still lets a local pass. At twenty, nobody at the back can hear the guide and the street is blocked.
What changes at fourteen
Past fourteen people, the guide has to raise their voice. People at the back start talking among themselves, and the group splits.
So we cap the walking tours at ten to fourteen, the food tours at eight and the private tours at the size you book.
What it costs us
We run more departures than we would with large groups. Some days the first tour sells out and the second is half empty. We prefer that.

data.title: What to bring on a cobbled tour
data.excerpt: Shoes matter more than anything else. A short list of what is worth carrying.

children.text: Cobbles are harder on feet than they look. Flat shoes with a thick sole will do more for you than anything else on this list.
Worth carrying
A refillable water bottle. There are drinking fountains on every tour route and the guide will show you where.
A light layer. Narrow streets are shaded and cool even in summer.
A small bag worn across the body. You will want both hands for the steps.
Not worth carrying
Large backpacks, heels and umbrellas with long spikes. The streets are tight.

data.title: How to eat well in the old city in two days
data.excerpt: Where to stand, what to order and what to skip if you only have a weekend.

children.text: You do not need a reservation for most of the good places. You need to arrive when the locals do.
Breakfast
Go to a bakery before eight. Order whatever the person in front of you ordered.
Lunch
Between one and two the market counters fill up. Arrive at half past twelve and you will find a seat.
Dinner
Locals eat late. If you are hungry at six, a cellar bar will feed you well and the food is simple.

data.title: The lantern lighters of Cooper's Row
data.excerpt: Until a hundred years ago one family lit every lamp in the quarter by hand. Some of the lamps are still there.

children.text: Each evening a man with a long pole walked from Lantern Square to Gate Square. He lit about sixty lamps and was done in under an hour.
The family
The job passed from father to son for four generations. The last lighter retired when the lamps were switched to electricity.
What is left
Some of the brackets are still on the walls. On the Lantern Evening Walk we stop under the oldest one.

data.title: A rainy day on our tours
data.excerpt: Tours run in light rain. What we change, and when we cancel.

children.text: Our tours go ahead in light rain. The old streets have arches and covered passages, so most of the route stays dry.
What we change
The guide may swap the viewpoints for the market, or skip the river walk. You still see the old city.
When we cancel
We cancel only if the weather is unsafe, for example lightning or high wind on the terraces. You get a full refund or a new date.

data.title: How we pick a meeting point
data.excerpt: Every tour starts at a square with somewhere to sit and a way to find us. That is harder than it sounds.

children.text: A good meeting point is easy to find from the main roads, has some shade and room for a group to stand without blocking anyone.
Our four squares
Lantern Square has the dry fountain and steps. Bell Tower Square has an arch where you can shelter. Gate Square is by the old gate. Mill Steps is at the river.
How to recognize us
A green flag and a guide wearing a lanyard. If you cannot find us, call the number on your confirmation email.
